claim: A transformer LM can be augmented with a “risk‑attention” module consisting of K additional attention heads and a learned risk summary token r that produces a bounded gating signal gt \in [0,1] used to re-weight next‑token logits away from tokens predicted to increase policy‑violation risk, and for at least three model families this architectural change will reduce the measured per‑response policy‑violation rate by ≥50% while keeping aggregate capability metrics within 2% relative of the baseline on a specified benchmark suite (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K, and MT‑Bench) under the same decoding policy.
subclaims: Can a transformer LM be augmented with a “risk-attention” module?
Does the “risk-attention” module consist of K additional attention heads?
Does the “risk-attention” module include a learned risk summary token r?
Does the learned risk summary token r produce a bounded gating signal gt?
Is the gating signal gt bounded within [0,1]?
Is the gating signal gt used to re-weight next-token logits away from tokens predicted to increase policy-violation risk?
For how many model families does this architectural change reduce the measured per-response policy-violation rate?
Does this architectural change reduce the measured per-response policy-violation rate by at least 50%?
Does this architectural change keep aggregate capability metrics within 2% relative to the baseline?
What benchmark suite is used to measure aggregate capability metrics?
Is the same decoding policy used when comparing the augmented model to the baseline?
baseline_experiments: To address subclaims 1-6, implement the proposed risk-attention augmentation in one small public transformer LM, such as Pythia-410M or GPT-2-medium, with K extra attention heads, a learned risk summary token r appended to the context, and a sigmoid-produced scalar or vector gate gt constrained to [0,1]. Train only the new module plus a small risk-token classifier/logit-reweighting layer on public safety data such as PKU-SafeRLHF, BeaverTails, Anthropic HH-RLHF harmlessness splits, or ToxicChat, while keeping the base LM fixed. Unit-test and log whether the architecture actually adds K heads, whether gradients update r, whether gt is always in [0,1], and whether high-risk token logits are reduced before decoding relative to the unmodified logits. If the module cannot be integrated without breaking generation, or if gt is not bounded or does not affect logits as specified, the architectural subclaims are not feasible as stated. If it integrates cleanly and produces calibrated lower logits for independently labeled risky continuations, the core mechanism is technically feasible and later efficacy experiments are justified. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a released implementation with training logs, ablation code, and tests proving the added heads, learned risk token, bounded gate, and logit reweighting behavior.

To address subclaims 6, 8, 9, 10, and 11, run a controlled single-family efficacy study comparing the augmented model from experiment 1 against the exact same base model under an identical decoding policy, such as temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9, max tokens fixed, and identical prompts. Evaluate per-response policy-violation rate on held-out public safety benchmarks, for example BeaverTails test, ToxicChat test, HarmBench or AdvBench prompts with a public safety classifier or human annotation protocol, and evaluate aggregate capability on public MMLU, GSM8K, and MT-Bench or an open MT-Bench-compatible judge. Use matched prompts and bootstrap confidence intervals to test whether violation rate falls by at least 50 percent while aggregate capability drops by no more than 2 percent relative to baseline. Include ablations for no gate, random gate, and classifier-only logit suppression to verify that any effect comes from the risk-attention design rather than decoding or a generic filter. If safety improves by at least 50 percent with under 2 percent capability loss, the main tradeoff is plausible for one family; if safety improves but capability drops substantially, the claim may need a weaker capability bound; if neither improves, the module is not promising. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a credible third-party benchmark report with matched decoding, public prompts, raw generations, and confidence intervals for the same model family.

To address subclaim 7 together with subclaims 8, 9, 10, and 11, replicate the best configuration from the first two experiments across at least three distinct public model families, for example Llama-3.2-1B or 3B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Gemma-2-2B or Pythia, using the same train/validation/test splits, the same decoding policy, and the same benchmark suite. For each family, compare baseline versus augmented model on held-out policy-violation prompts and on MMLU, GSM8K, and MT-Bench, reporting per-family and aggregate relative changes with confidence intervals. The claim is supported only if at least three families independently achieve at least a 50 percent reduction in measured per-response policy violations while staying within 2 percent relative capability loss; mixed results would identify architecture- or scale-dependent limits; consistent failure would refute the broad claim. Earlier experiments should determine K, training recipe, and evaluation thresholds before this expensive replication. This experiment could be made unnecessary by public reproducible results across three model families, including checkpoints or adapters, benchmark scripts, decoding configs, and raw outputs.
method_experiments: To address subclaims 1–6, implement a minimal risk-attention augmentation in three open-weight transformer LM families, such as Llama-2/3, Mistral, and Qwen or Gemma. Add K extra attention heads in selected upper layers, prepend or append a learned risk summary token r, compute a scalar gate g_t = sigmoid(W h_r,t + b) so that g_t is provably in [0,1], and reweight next-token logits using a learned token-risk vector or risk classifier, e.g. logits'_t[v] = logits_t[v] - lambda * g_t * risk_t[v]. Train only the new module, or the new module plus LoRA adapters, on public labeled safety data such as ToxicChat, Aegis-2.0-Safety, BeaverTails/Beaver, SafeRLHF, or SALAD-Base. Verify by unit tests and logging that: the additional heads are active, r receives attention from normal tokens, g_t is bounded, and tokens labeled or predicted as policy-risk-increasing receive lower post-gate logits. Include ablations with no extra heads, no r token, and no logit reweighting. If the module cannot be integrated without breaking generation, if g_t is not bounded, or if risky-token logits are not selectively reduced, the architectural subclaims are infeasible. If all checks pass across model families, the architecture is feasible enough for efficacy testing. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released source code, checkpoints, and logs showing the exact K-head/r-token/gating implementation and its logit effects.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 11, run a controlled safety evaluation comparing each baseline model family to its risk-attention-augmented counterpart under the exact same decoding policy, for example temperature, top-p, max tokens, system prompt, and refusal policy held fixed. Use public adversarial and safety benchmarks such as HarmBench, SALAD-Bench or SALAD-Enhance-Test, XSafety, MultiJail, ToxicChat, Aegis-2.0-Safety, and JailbreakHub; define per-response policy violation using a prespecified judge ensemble, for example Llama Guard, Aegis, MD-Judge, plus human audit on a stratified subset. For each of at least three families, estimate baseline and augmented violation rates with bootstrap confidence intervals and test whether the relative reduction is at least 50%, e.g. (rate_base - rate_aug)/rate_base >= 0.50, without relying on increased refusal to benign prompts. If all three families meet or exceed 50% reduction with non-overlapping or statistically persuasive confidence intervals, the central safety-effect subclaim is supported; if only one or two families pass, the 'at least three model families' part fails; if reductions are small or caused mainly by blanket refusals, the claim is not supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by independent benchmark reports that publish prompts, generations, judges, decoding settings, and per-family violation-rate confidence intervals for the same architecture.

To address subclaims 9, 10, and 11, evaluate capability retention for the same baseline and augmented checkpoints from the safety experiment, again under the same decoding policy except where a benchmark mandates deterministic decoding. Use public benchmark implementations and datasets for MMLU, GSM8K, and MT-Bench, optionally adding ARC, HellaSwag, HumanEval, or AlpacaEval 2.0 as sensitivity checks. Compute an aggregate capability score by pre-registering the metric normalization, for example mean relative score over MMLU accuracy, GSM8K exact match, and MT-Bench judge score. Compare augmented versus baseline per model family and overall, requiring the augmented model to remain within 2% relative of baseline aggregate capability. If safety improves but MMLU/GSM8K/MT-Bench fall by more than 2%, the claimed tradeoff fails; if scores remain within 2% for all or most of the three families while experiment 2 also passes, the feasibility claim is strongly supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by reproducible evaluation artifacts from a trusted harness, including exact benchmark versions, prompts, decoding parameters, raw outputs, and scoring scripts.
